1.pericope_label: Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations

debates.q: Can the psalm really be Moses’?

sides.view: No — men then lived far beyond the seventy years the psalm names as the limit
Yes — scarcely any ancient memorial so brilliantly justifies its own tradition
The name is taken as given, and read of the minister of the old covenant

debates.q: What does the thousand years teach?

sides.view: That length of time in the grave is no objection to the resurrection
Nothing arithmetical; the verse contrasts divine unchangeableness with human brevity
That time seems long to come and very short when past

outliers.view: Argues against the psalm’s own title from the recorded ages of Moses and his contemporaries
Notes that the verse was already being used for millenarian computation in apostolic times, and declines that use

5.pericope_label: Thou carriest them away as with a flood; they are as a sleep

debates.q: Is the consumption universal or national?

sides.view: National — the change to the plural makes it a dirge over the departed glory of Israel
National, a confession of the sentence Israel lay under in a special manner
Universal — death entered because men fell, and disease proves the defection

debates.q: What is the light of the divine countenance here?

sides.view: Not favour but a body of light — the sun, or eye, of his countenance
A candle carried into a dark place, discovering what is hidden
The judgments by which secret sins are brought to light

outliers.view: Assembles the whole passage into one system of figures — life a stream, youth morning, age evening, death sleep, resurrection the spring flowers
Would render the phrase our secret character rather than our secret sins, keeping the singular of the original

9.pericope_label: For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told

debates.q: What do we spend our years as?

sides.view: Like a groan — the versions have spider, but no Hebrew copy supports it
A murmur, or moan of sadness; some render it thought

debates.q: What is asked in teach us to number our days?

sides.view: Nothing of the kind — God is the reckoner, and the received rendering is unsupportable
Not arithmetic but numbering them as if the present were the last
A child’s exercise for which the best of men still need teaching
An excellent art, and a consideration of the speediness of death

outliers.view: Renders the clause we consume our years like a groan, and reports a mediaeval paraphrase that makes them the spider’s vain webs
Rejects the rendering on which the whole devotional tradition of the verse rests, calling it neither intelligible nor supportable

13.pericope_label: Return, O Lord: the prayer for mercy, for gladness proportioned to the affliction, and for the establishing of the work of their hands

schools.summary: Gill reads the closing petitions doctrinally, taking the morning of mercy as the gospel dispensation and Christ himself, and the work to be shown as providence, redemption, or the inward work of grace.

Clarke sets the prayer in the return from captivity and the rebuilding of the temple, and notes the textual state of the closing repetition; Wesley reduces the petitions to their plainest sense and asks that God work in his people as well as for them.
Ellicott renders turn rather than return and have pity rather than repent, and reads the close as a prayer of a particular epoch for the suffering community rather than for the poet himself.

debates: What does satisfying us early ask for? Gill takes the morning as the morning of the gospel dispensation and of Christ, the mercy promised to the fathers, while Ellicott keeps it to the morning of new hope after a night of affliction, Clarke to a mercy shining now, and Wesley to a single word, speedily.

What occasion does the closing prayer belong to? Clarke dates it to seventy years of captivity and the rebuilding of the temple against Samaritan obstruction, and Ellicott to some particular epoch of national suffering, while Gill reads the same petitions as providence, redemption and the inward work of grace without an occasion.
outliers: Ellicott observes that the poet, unlike Hezekiah, does not turn his meditation on the shortness of life into a prayer for his own lengthened days but into a prayer for the community.
Clarke leaves the text of the last clause open, reporting that the repetition is absent from three of Kennicott’s manuscripts and from the Targum, the Septuagint and the Ethiopic.
themes: prayer for God to turn and have pity
the morning of mercy after a night of affliction
gladness measured against the days of affliction
the work of God made visible to servants and children
the establishing of the work of human hands
